summary: Gives the details for using the DES cipher to encrypt packets carried over PPP, in a second version of the specification. It replaces RFC 1969. DES is now considered weak. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: PPP is a phone-line style connection between two computers. This document says how to scramble packets on that line with an old code that is now easy to break.

questions: how does ppp des encryption work
what is the ecp dese option
subtitle: How to encrypt PPP packets with DES in chaining mode, with a nonce, sequence numbers and recovery from lost packets.

tldr.problem: The PPP Encryption Control Protocol can negotiate encryption, but something has to spell out one concrete algorithm so two PPP implementations can scramble their traffic the same way.
tldr.mechanism: Each PPP packet is padded to a multiple of 8 bytes and encrypted with DES in Cipher Block Chaining mode under a 56-bit shared key. The first block is seeded from an 8-byte nonce sent during negotiation, and a 16-bit sequence number keeps both ends in step.
tldr.outcome: It gives confidentiality only, with no integrity or authentication, and it replaces RFC 1969 with a new option type and mandatory padding of every packet.

today: RFC 2419 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 1969, and the unit metadata lists no later RFC that replaces or updates it. The RFC itself warns that any limitations of the DES cipher apply to this scheme.

sections.title: Introduction and Overview
sections.content:
RFC 2419 describes DESE-bis, the second version of the PPP DES Encryption Protocol. It has two goals: to show how a "data" or "bearer" protocol is specified inside the generic PPP Encryption Control Protocol (ECP), and to give PPP implementations at least one commonly understood way of sending data securely.

The encryptor takes a PPP packet including its protocol field, encrypts it, and places the resulting ciphertext and an explicit sequence number in the information field of another PPP packet. The decryptor reverses the process and treats the result as if it had arrived directly on the interface.

How both sides come to know the shared secret is outside the scope of the document. Usually it is configured by hand, and if the secret can be deduced from the traffic, no privacy is guaranteed. The RFC says DES is well studied and widely implemented, but designed for hardware and so relatively expensive in software.
sections.eli5: Both computers need to know the same secret password first. This document only explains how to scramble the packets once they both have it.

sections.title: The DESE Configuration Option
sections.content:
ECP handles the negotiation, so this specification only adds one configuration option. Offering the ECP DESE Configuration Option says that the sender is willing to decrypt traffic this way, and asks its peer to encrypt packets in this manner.

The option has Type = 3, Length = 10 and an 8-byte Initial Nonce. The old value 1 belonged to the previous DESE specification. Implementations of this RFC MUST NOT offer value 1 and MUST configure-reject it if a peer sends it.

The nonce is used by the peer to encrypt the first packet after the sender reaches the Opened state. To guard against replay, an implementation SHOULD offer a different value in each ECP negotiation. The RFC suggests seconds since 1 January 1970 in the upper 32 bits and nanoseconds since the last second in the lower 32 bits.
sections.eli5: Before talking in code, each side hands the other a fresh random-looking starting number. Using a new one every time stops someone from replaying an old conversation.

sections.title: The DESE Packet Format
sections.content:
A DESE packet starts with the usual PPP Address and Control bytes, which MUST be present unless Address and Control Field Compression (ACFC) was negotiated. Next is a protocol field with value 0x0053 or 0x0055; the leading zero MAY be absent if Protocol Field Compression (PFC) was negotiated.

The value 0x55 means the ciphertext includes Multilink Protocol headers, and it REQUIRES the Individual Link Encryption Control Protocol to have reached the Opened state. Then come a 16-bit sequence number (sent as a high byte and a low byte) and the ciphertext.

The encryptor assigns sequence numbers one after another, starting at 0 for the first packet sent once ECP is Opened.
sections.eli5: Each scrambled packet carries a label saying it is scrambled, a counter so the receiver knows the order, and then the scrambled message itself.

sections.title: Encryption, Padding and Chaining
sections.content:
Once ECP is Opened, the sender MUST NOT encrypt LCP packets or ECP packets. The encryption covers the PPP Protocol and Information fields, never the Address and Control fields, whether or not ACFC was negotiated. If the async control character map is in use, mapping is applied after encryption.

DES works on 8-octet blocks, so every plaintext is padded. The RFC applies a Self-Describing Padding scheme to ALL packets, with a maximum pad value of 8, independent of the LCP SDP option. Plaintext that is not a multiple of 8 octets MUST be padded with octets 1, 2, 3 and so on up to 7. A plaintext that is already a multiple of 8 needs an extra 8 octets (1 to 8) if its last octet has a value from 1 through 8. After decryption only the last octet needs checking to know how much padding to strip, but the peer SHOULD discard the frame if the padding does not match the scheme.

The cipher is DES in Cipher Block Chaining mode with a 56-bit key k. With E[k] as encryption and ^ as exclusive-or on 64-bit blocks, each ciphertext block is C[i] = E[k](P[i] ^ C[i-1]). For the first packet, C[0] is E[k] applied to the peer's Initial Nonce; otherwise it is the final ciphertext block of the previous packet. Decryption is P[i] = C[i-1] ^ D[k](C[i]).

Chaining makes identical plaintext produce different ciphertext, which complicates analysis. Because chaining runs across packet boundaries, both sides must agree on packet order, which is why the sequence number exists.
sections.eli5: Each chunk of the message is mixed with the scrambled chunk before it, like a chain, so the same words never look the same twice. Short messages get filler added to fill the last chunk.

sections.title: Packet Loss and MRU
sections.content:
A gap in sequence numbers reveals a lost packet. Suppose packet N - 1 is lost but packets N and N + 1 arrive. Packet N cannot be decrypted, because its C[0] is the last ciphertext block of packet N - 1. Packet N + 1 and later packets can be decoded normally, since they only need the last ciphertext block of the previous packet, and packet N was received.

Padding, the extra protocol field and the 2-byte sequence number make packets grow. The RFC's example: with PFC negotiated and an MRU that was an exact multiple of 8, a full-sized packet plus a one-byte protocol field needs 7 more bytes of padding, and the sequence number adds 2, so the DESE information field is 10 bytes larger. Negotiating DESE does not by itself raise the MRU.
sections.eli5: If one page of a chained message goes missing, the very next page is unreadable, but the one after that works again because it only needs the page that did arrive.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC provides confidentiality only. It describes no integrity, authentication or non-repudiation. It does not guarantee that a received message was not changed in transit by replay, cut-and-paste or active tampering, and it does not authenticate the source of a packet.

It also relies on outside, unspecified methods for authentication and for getting shared secrets. It proposes no new privacy technology, only a convention for applying DES to PPP traffic, so any weakness in secret handling or in the DES cipher applies directly.
sections.eli5: The code hides what you say but does not prove who said it, and anyone could swap pieces around. It is only as strong as the secret and the old cipher behind it.

sections.title: Differences from RFC 1969
sections.content:
RFC 1969 padded only "specifically identified protocols" and exempted protocols with an explicit length, such as non-VJ-compressed IP, XNS and CLNP. This RFC pads ALL packets, makes the method independent of the LCP SDP option, and fixes the maximum pad at 8.

Since the change could cause a packet sent under the old rules to be misread, a new option type number (3) was assigned. The remaining edits are editorial, and the document was made a standards track specification.
sections.eli5: The old version only added filler sometimes. The new one always does, so it gets a new label to avoid mix-ups.

fields.name: Address
fields.desc: PPP address; may be omitted if ACFC is negotiated.

fields.name: Control
fields.desc: PPP control; may be omitted if ACFC is negotiated.
Leading zero of the protocol field; may be absent with PFC.

fields.name: Protocol ID
fields.desc: 0x53, or 0x55 when ciphertext includes Multilink headers.

fields.name: Seq. No. High
fields.desc: High byte of the 16-bit sequence number.

fields.name: Seq. No. Low
fields.desc: Low byte of the 16-bit sequence number.

fields.name: Initial Nonce (remaining 48 bits)
fields.desc: Rest of the 8-byte nonce used to encrypt the first packet.
